uncited: This family of methods reduces the geometric complexity or improves the quality of the isosurface mesh $M$ generated by parent algorithms like Marching Cubes.

While the parent algorithm fixes the initial topology via lookup tables, these methods modify geometric properties (vertex positions) or topological complexity (triangle count) to balance rendering performance, storage requirements, and visual fidelity [Shared principles].

All methods in this family operate on the mesh $M$ generated by the parent algorithm, which consists of vertices $V$, triangles $T$, and adjacency information derived from the `edgeTable` and `triangleTable` [Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling](10327-lookup-table-and-ambiguity-handling.md).

The core shared principle is that the initial topology (connectivity) is fixed by the parent's lookup tables, but the geometric properties (vertex positions, triangle count, or boundary status) are modified.

**Geometric Refinement:** Adjusting vertex positions to minimize the distance to the true isosurface $f(\mathbf{x}) = I$ or to improve mesh quality metrics (e.g., aspect ratio) [Vertex Position Optimization and Error Minimization](10991-vertex-position-optimization-and-error-minimization.md).

**Complexity Reduction:** Collapsing edges or merging coplanar triangles to reduce the triangle count $|T|$ while preserving visual fidelity and manifoldness [Mesh Simplification and Optimization](8588-mesh-simplification-and-optimization.md).

**Boundary Closure:** Identifying open boundary edges (edges shared by only one triangle) and triangulating caps to ensure the mesh is a closed 2-manifold [Marching Cubes Boundary Cap](13166-marching-cubes-boundary-cap.md).
The foundational work on Marching Cubes was introduced by Lorensen and Cline in 1987 [Loren87].
